There is no other logic. To adapt the 1018 pipeline to your own documents, edit these descriptions. 1019 1020 [code omitted] 1021 1022 Everything below is plumbing: build the questions, send one request, read the answers back. 1023 If the type comes back `heading`, the renderer needs a heading level; if `list_item`, 1024 whether order matters; if `callout`, which kind. The types are not known yet, and waiting 1025 for them would mean a third round trip, so the companion questions are asked up front in 1026 the same request. Most of these answers are never read: the step probability of a paragraph 1027 means nothing and is simply ignored. An extra question adds little, since the state is 1028 most of the tokens and is sent once either way, while an extra round trip adds a full 1029 request of latency. 1030 1031 ```python expandable theme={null} 1032 HEADING_MAX_CHARS = 90 # longer blocks can't render as headings, so don't ask 1033 1034 def classify_questions(texts: list[str]) -> dict: 1035 questions = {} 1036 for i, text in enumerate(texts): 1037 bid = block_id(i) 1038 questions[f"type_{bid}"] = Choice( 1039 instructions=f"What kind of content is block {bid}?", criteria=TYPE_CRITERIA 1040 ) 1041 if len(text) <= HEADING_MAX_CHARS: 1042 questions[f"hlevel_{bid}"] = Choice( 1043 instructions=f"As a heading, what level would block {bid} occupy in this document's structure?", 1044 criteria=HLEVEL_CRITERIA, 1045 ) 1046 questions[f"step_{bid}"] = Noul( 1047 instructions=f"Is block {bid} an instruction in a sequence where the order of the items matters?", 1048 criteria=NoulCriteria( 1049 true="It is one step of a procedure - the items around it must happen in order", 1050 false="Order is irrelevant - it is a loose collection, or not a list item at all", 1051 ), 1052 ) 1053 questions[f"callout_{bid}"] = Choice( 1054 instructions=f"What kind of aside is block {bid}?", criteria=CALLOUT_CRITERIA 1055 ) 1056 return questions 1057 1058 @json_cache 1059 def classify(texts: list[str], gaps: list[bool]) -> dict: 1060 tagged = tag([{"text": t, "gap": g} for t, g in zip(texts, gaps)], "B") 1061 questions = classify_questions(texts) 1062 started = perf_counter() 1063 response = client.system_one(state=tagged, questions=questions, model=TYPESAFE_MODEL) 1064 judgments = [] 1065 for i in range(len(texts)): 1066 bid = block_id(i) 1067 type_answer = response.answers[f"type_{bid}"] 1068 hlevel = response.answers.get(f"hlevel_{bid}") 1069 judgments.append( 1070 { 1071 "type": type_answer.choice, 1072 "confidence": type_answer.confidence, 1073 "probabilities": type_answer.probabilities, 1074 "hlevel": hlevel.choice if hlevel else "section", 1075 "step": response.answers[f"step_{bid}"].noul, 1076 "callout": response.answers[f"callout_{bid}"].choice, 1077 } 1078 ) 1079 return { 1080 "judgments": judgments, 1081 "n_questions": len(questions), 1082 "seconds": round(perf_counter() - started, 2), 1083 "usage": [response.usage.input_tokens, response.usage.output_tokens], 1084 } 1085 1086 classified = classify([b["text"] for b in blocks], [b["gap"] for b in blocks]) 1087 for block, judgment in zip(blocks, classified["judgments"]): 1088 block.update(judgment) 1089 print(f"{classified['n_questions']} questions about {len(blocks)} blocks, one request, " 1090 f"{classified['seconds']}s\n") 1091 ...[truncated] 1092 ``` 1093 1094 ``` 1095 62 questions about 17 blocks, one request, 0.51s 1096 1097 block type conf companion used text 1098 B000 heading 0.99 level=title Migration to the new build system 1099 B001 paragraph 0.98 - Hi everyone, quick heads up about the build sy 1100 B002 heading 0.75 level=section What changes for you 1101 B003 paragraph 0.89 - The old make targets keep working until the en 1102 B004 code 1.00 - bun run build 1103 B005 paragraph 0.90 - Generated artifacts no longer need to be commi 1104 B006 paragraph 0.43 - The cutover touches three teams, so check whet 1105 B007 list_item 0.99 step=0.15 The platform team 1106 B008 list_item 1.00 step=0.16 The web client team 1107 B009 list_item 0.99 step=0.12 Whoever still owns the release tooling 1108 B010 heading 0.96 level=section Things to do before Monday 1109 B011 list_item 0.98 step=0.86 Update your local toolchain to version 2.4 or 1110 B012 list_item 0.99 step=0.87 Delete the old build cache directory 1111 B013 list_item 0.92 step=0.90 Run the doctor script and fix anything it flag 1112 B014 callout 0.65 kind=warning If the doctor script reports a red result on t 1113 B015 quote 0.99 - As Dana put it in the kickoff, "a migration no 1114 B016 paragraph 0.92 - Thanks, and shout if anything looks off. 1115 ``` 1116 1117 Every block's judgment is in that table, and the companion column shows the up-front 1118 answers being put to use: the three "Things to do before Monday" lines carry step 1119 probabilities near 0.9 (they will render as a numbered list), the three team lines sit 1120 near 0.1 (bulleted), and the unmarked warning about the doctor script was classified as 1121 a callout of kind `warning`. The appendix looks at the one block the model was unsure 1122 about. 1123 1124 ## Rendering 1125 1126 Code assembles the page from the judgments. Consecutive list items become one list, 1127 numbered when the mean of the items' step probabilities is at least 0.5. That threshold 1128 is a 1129 group-level decision no single question asked directly. 1130 1131 ````python expandable theme={null} 1132 STEP_THRESHOLD = 0.5 1133 HEADING_MARK = {"title": "#", "section": "##", "subsection": "###"} 1134 CALLOUT_MARK = {"note": "NOTE", "tip": "TIP", "warning": "WARNING"} 1135 1136 def to_markdown(blocks: list[dict]) -> str: 1137 groups = [] 1138 for b in blocks: 1139 if b["type"] in ("list_item", "code") and groups and groups[-1][0] == b["type"]: 1140 groups[-1][1].append(b) 1141 else: 1142 groups.append((b["type"], [b])) 1143 parts = [] 1144 for kind, items in groups: 1145 if kind == "list_item": 1146 ordered = sum(b["step"] for b in items) / len(items) >= STEP_THRESHOLD 1147 parts.append("\n".join( 1148 f"{n + 1}. {b['text']}" if ordered else f"- {b['text']}" 1149 for n, b in enumerate(items) 1150 )) 1151 elif kind == "code": 1152 parts.append("```\n" + "\n".join(b["text"] for b in items) + "\n```") 1153 elif kind == "heading": 1154 parts.append(f"{HEADING_MARK[items[0]['hlevel']]} {items[0]['text']}") 1155 elif kind == "quote": 1156 parts.append(f"> {items[0]['text']}") 1157 elif kind == "callout": 1158 parts.append(f"> [!{CALLOUT_MARK[items[0]['callout']]}]\n> {items[0]['text']}") 1159 else: 1160 parts.append(items[0]["text"]) 1161 return "\n\n".join(parts) + "\n" 1162 1163 markdown = to_markdown(blocks) 1164 print(markdown) 1165 ```` 1166 1167 ````text expandable theme={null} 1168 # Migration to the new build system 1169 1170 Hi everyone, quick heads up about the build system migration that is happening next week. We have been running the new pipeline in shadow mode for three weeks and the results look solid, so it is time to make the switch for real. 1171 1172 ## What changes for you 1173 1174 The old make targets keep working until the end of the month. The new entrypoint is a single command that wraps everything, including the docs build that used to be separate. 1175 1176 ``` 1177 bun run build 1178 ``` 1179 1180 Generated artifacts no longer need to be committed. The new pipeline uploads them to the registry automatically, and checking them in just creates merge conflicts. 1181 1182 The cutover touches three teams, so check whether you are on this list before you plan anything for Monday: 1183 1184 - The platform team 1185 - The web client team 1186 - Whoever still owns the release tooling 1187 1188 ## Things to do before Monday 1189 1190 1. Update your local toolchain to version 2.4 or later 1191 2. Delete the old build cache directory 1192 3. Run the doctor script and fix anything it flags 1193 1194 > [!WARNING] 1195 > If the doctor script reports a red result on the toolchain check, do not proceed with the migration. Ping the infra channel first and we will sort it out together. 1196 1197 > As Dana put it in the kickoff, "a migration nobody notices is the only kind worth shipping." 1198 1199 Thanks, and shout if anything looks off. 1200 ```` 1201 1202 Every word above is from the input. The pipeline only chose boundaries, types, and 1203 markup. 1204 1205 ## Open it in the playground 1206 1207 This share link holds the stitched blocks and the full pass-2 question set. Open it to 1208 re-run the classification live. 1209 1210 [code omitted] 1211 1212 *** 1213 1214 # Appendix 1215 1216 ## Cost and latency 1217 1218 [code omitted] 1219 1220 ``` 1221 pass 1 16 questions 0.32s 1222 pass 2 62 questions 0.51s 1223 total 10,211 tokens 0.8s $0.0003 1224 ``` 1225 1226 Two round trips, 10,211 tokens, 0.8s, \$0.0015. 1227 1228 ## Where the join thresholds come from 1229 1230 The per-line join probabilities from pass 1: 1231 1232 [code omitted] 1233 1234 ``` 1235 join line 1236 L000| Migration to the new build system 1237 L001| Hi everyone, quick heads up about the build system migration that 1238 0.77 L002| happening next week. We have been running the new pipeline in shad 1239 0.62 L003| mode for three weeks and the results look solid, so it is time to 1240 0.39 L004| make the switch for real. 1241 L005| What changes for you 1242 L006| The old make targets keep working until the end of the month. The 1243 0.42 L007| entrypoint is a single command that wraps everything, including th 1244 0.59 L008| docs build that used to be separate. 1245 L009| bun run build 1246 L010| Generated artifacts no longer need to be committed. The new pipeli 1247 0.48 L011| uploads them to the registry automatically, and checking them in 1248 0.40 L012| just creates merge conflicts. 1249 L013| The cutover touches three teams, so check whether you are on this 1250 0.50 L014| list before you plan anything for Monday: 1251 0.22 L015| The platform team 1252 0.11 L016| The web client team 1253 0.12 L017| Whoever still owns the release tooling 1254 ``` 1255 1256 The probabilities land in two separate bands: line breaks that split a sentence score 1257 0.39 and up, breaks the author meant score close to zero. But where to put the cutoff 1258 between the bands depends on **how the previous line ends**, a fact code can read 1259 directly: 1260 1261 * After a *dangling* line (one with no sentence-ending punctuation), anything at 0.2 or 1262 above counts as a continuation. True continuations score as low as 0.39 here (`L004| 1263 make the switch for real.`), so a single cautious cutoff at 0.5 would break up healthy 1264 paragraphs. 1265 * After *terminal* punctuation (a character that ends a sentence or clause: `.` `!` `?` 1266 `:` `;`), the cutoff rises to 0.5. The memo's team list shows why: `L015| The platform 1267 team` follows a colon and scores 0.22. That is a low but nonzero "this continues the 1268 sentence" signal, and it would clear the 0.2 cutoff and merge the list into the 1269 sentence 1270 introducing it. No single threshold works for both cases; once code checks the 1271 punctuation first, the two bands separate. 1272 1273 ## Why the question is "mid-sentence" and not "same paragraph" 1274 1275 The first version of this pipeline asked the obvious question: "are these two lines part 1276 of the same paragraph?" It failed in a specific way. A run of short lines under a 1277 heading (a list typed without bullets) *is* a paragraph in the loose sense: the lines sit 1278 together and share a topic. Asked about paragraphs, the model says yes to every pair, and 1279 the stitch pass merges the whole list into one long block. 1280 1281 Same document, same request shape, only the wording changed: 1282 1283 ```python theme={null} 1284 def naive_join_question(i: int) -> Noul: 1285 return Noul( 1286 instructions=f"Are lines {line_id(i - 1)} and {line_id(i)} part of the same paragraph?", 1287 criteria=NoulCriteria( 1288 true="The two lines belong to the same paragraph of running text", 1289 false="The two lines belong to different paragraphs or different pieces of content", 1290 ), 1291 )

A lot of data exists as structured hierarchies, such as a taxonomies, filesystem hierarchies, website structures, codebases, org charts, biological ontologies, LLM skills, moderation policies, etc. The goal of Hierarchical Classification is to traverse the hierarchy to the correct leaf node, which is the final classification. This is a perfect fit for typesafe's `Choice` primitive. We find the most probable leaf by classifying the document at each node (starting at the root), and then iteratively proceeding to the next most-probable node until we end at a leaf (**Greedy Search**). The parallel nature of the API also lets us explore multiple paths with parallel questions using **Beam Search** to improve performance. The cookbook's TypeSafe API calls each simultaneously evaluate `K` paths of the hierarchy. Beam search keeps the best `K` paths by a geometric-mean edge probability: `product(edge_probabilities) ** (1 / decisions)`, and prunes the rest. The probability is length-normalized so that shallow and deep leaves are compared fairly. Decomposing the problem into a hierarchy like this has benefits of its own: * Observability * identify which nodes your misclassifications occur most in * measure the number of times each node and edge is traversed * Testability * unit test and measure the impact of hierarchy updates on classification performance * ### Hierarchies used in this cookbook * **[CPC 2026.05](https://www.cooperativepatentclassification.org/sites/default/files/cpc/bulk/CPCSchemeXML202605.zip):** patent subject matter, from broad technology sections to narrow inventions. * **[Shopify 2026-02](https://github.com/Shopify/product-taxonomy/blob/v2026-02/dist/en/categories.txt):** retail product categories, from store departments to specific product types. * **[MeSH 2026](https://nlmpubs.nlm.nih.gov/projects/mesh/MESH_FILES/xmlmesh/desc2026.zip):** biomedical subjects from broad domains to specific conditions. MeSH is a DAG, so one descriptor can appear under multiple parents; this demo expands its official tree-number paths. * **CookSafe files:** TypeSafe's cookbook repository hierarchy, searched from folders to source files. ### Methods * **Greedy search:** choose the highest-probability child and discard every alternative. One early mistake cannot be recovered. * **Beam search:** retain `K` plausible paths and classify every frontier in parallel. Deeper evidence can repair an ambiguous early decision. The leaf of the path with the highest geometric-mean probability is the final classification. * **TypeSafe Choice:** every node is a `Choice` question whose full probability distribution is its edges. Each path of the beam runs as parallel questions, so extra exploration adds little wall-clock latency. * **Formula:** * `path_score = product(edge_probabilities) ** (1 / decisions)` * used for pruning and comparing paths * `separation = top_path_score / second_path_score` * useful metric, but not used for pruning * the ratio compares the top path's geometric mean against its nearest rival. * Near `1×` is ambiguous * A large ratio means clear separation. * **Notes on metrics:** * a different metric such as `min(top_prob/second_top_prob)` which would optimize for paths that have very clear decisions at every node. * use `exp(mean(log(probs)))` instead of `product(edge_probabilities) ** (1 / decisions)` to avoid precision errors for hierarchies that are very deep (eg >10 layers) ## Load and visualize the example hierarchies These helpers download pinned taxonomy sources, parse them into direct-child trees, and render each search traversal as a static SVG. [code omitted] ## Implement greedy and beam search Each sibling set becomes one `Choice` question in the next section, which also implements both traversal strategies and keeps the probabilities the static diagrams need. ```python expandable theme={null} HIERARCHIES = load_hierarchies() MODEL, BEAM_WIDTH, MAX_DEPTH, EPSILON = "jev-1.12", 3, 12, 1e-9 client = TypeSafeClient( api_key=os.environ["TYPESAFE_API_KEY"], retry=RetryPolicy(max_retries=5, backoff_initial=1.0, backoff_max=20.0), ) json_cache = JsonCache(Path("json_cache.json")) @json_cache def choose(state: str, labels: tuple[str, ...]) -> dict[str, float]: """Ask one atomic direct-child question and return its distribution.""" if len(labels) == 1: return {labels[0]: 1.0} question, keys = child_question(labels) response = client.system_one( state=state, questions={"child": question}, model=MODEL ) probabilities = response.answers["child"].probabilities return {label: probabilities[key] for key, label in keys.items()} def child_question(labels: tuple[str, ...]) -> tuple[Choice, dict[str, str]]: """Build the direct-child Choice and its reversible option mapping.""" keys = {f"c{i}": label for i, label in enumerate(labels)} question = Choice( instructions="Which direct child category best matches this document?", criteria=keys, ) return question, keys def extend_candidate( candidate: dict, label: str, probabilities: dict[str, float] ) -> dict: """Append one edge and recompute its geometric-mean path score.""" is_decision: bool = len(probabilities) > 1 # Use log space for very deep trees to avoid floating-point precision loss. probability_product: float = candidate["probability_product"] * ( max(probabilities[label], EPSILON) if is_decision else 1.0 ) decision_count: int = candidate["decision_count"] + is_decision return { "path": candidate["path"] + (label,), "probability_product": probability_product, "decision_count": decision_count, "score": probability_product ** (1 / decision_count) if decision_count else 1.0, } def choice_record(path: tuple[str, ...], probabilities: dict[str, float]) -> dict: """Package one sibling decision for the traversal diagram.""" return {"parent": path, "probabilities": probabilities} def beam_search(hierarchy: Hierarchy) -> dict: """Parallel width-three beam search using geometric-mean probability.""" beam = [{"path": (), "probability_product": 1.0, "decision_count": 0, "score": 1.0}] records, retained_paths = [], {()} for _ in range(MAX_DEPTH): expandable = [ candidate for candidate in beam ...[truncated] ``` ## Compare the methods Run both strategies on four labeled examples, compare their leaves against the expected classifications, and visualize the routes they explored. [code omitted] ## Results Each example has a known expected leaf. Beam search matched 4 of 4 expected leaves; greedy search matched 2 of 4. Keeping three paths recovered the expected classification for CPC patents, Shopify products. | Hierarchy | Expected leaf | Greedy leaf | Beam K=3 leaf | Greedy correct | Beam correct | | ------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------- | -------------- | ------------ | | CPC patents | A01K31/12 Perches for poultry or birds, e.g. roosts | E99Z99/00 Subject matter not otherwise provided for in this section | A01K31/12 Perches for poultry or birds, e.g. roosts | no | yes | | Shopify products | Cat Window Beds & Perches | Pet Chairs | Cat Window Beds & Perches | no | yes | | MeSH biomedical subjects | C06.405.469.432.500 Crohn Disease | C06.405.469.432.500 Crohn Disease | C06.405.469.432.500 Crohn Disease | yes | yes | | CookSafe files | retrievers.py | retrievers.py | retrievers.py | yes | yes | The diagrams show why the methods differ. Orange marks the greedy route, green marks the winning beam route, purple marks other retained paths, and dashed edges were pruned. ### CPC patents ### Shopify products ### MeSH biomedical subjects ### CookSafe files ################ cookbooks/sde_cascade.md ################ # SDE cascade > Uses a 2-stage structured-data-extraction cascade (mini → verify → reasoning) to get most of the quality of a big reasoning model at a fraction of the cost. * Overview * big reasoning models extract structured data well, but are slow and expensive * small models are cheap, but make mistakes * a *cascade* gets most of the quality at a fraction of the cost * the models we use, and their price (\$ per 1M tokens, input / output; standard rates checked September 15, 2026): * rung 0 (mini): [`gpt-5.4-mini`](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/models/gpt-5.4-mini) at \$0.75 / \$4.50 * rung 1 (reasoning): [`gpt-5.5`](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/models/gpt-5.5) at \$5.00 / \$30.00 (roughly 7x the mini) * verifier: TypeSafe `jev-1.12` at \$0.042 / \$0.00 (output tokens are free; [published Jev pricing](https://typesafe.ai/blog/introducing-system-one-models-and-jev)) * Algorithm 1. **Extract** with a cheap/small model. 2. **Verify** with **TypeSafe** primitives: a per-field yes/no ("Noul question") question * (e.g. "is this value absent from the source?", "was it lifted from unrelated text?"), each returning P(something is wrong). 3. **Escalate** to an expensive reasoning model if a verifier signal fires; otherwise keep the cheap answer. * This Cookbook * walks one real example end-to-end, then shows the tradeoff across 100 prompts * note: the two extraction rungs use text-mode OpenAI * we do *not* use structured outputs, tool calls, or json mode, because: * a *schema following* mistake is not the mistake we expect an LLM to make (it's easy to make synthetic data for this) * if an LLM does fail to follow the schema, it's almost always very confused, so constrained decoding doesn't fix the underlying issue * we encourage you to try them though! ## Setup * install the dependencies (the TypeSafe verifier client is served from TypeSafe's package index): ```bash theme={null} pip install openai datasets jsonschema ipython "typesafe-sdk>=0.5.7" cooksafe --extra-index-url https://pypi.typesafe.ai/ ``` * then set `OPENAI_API_KEY` and `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` in your environment [code omitted] ## Step 1: the data We choose a huggingface dataset called scrapegraphai [code omitted] ```text expandable theme={null} PROMPT =========== Find registration open date fall semester for New York University in New York, NY for the 2024-2025 school year. SCHEMA =========== { "properties": { "registration_open_date": { "description": "The date that registration opens for the fall semester. MUST be in the format mm/dd/yyyy. For example, for a college in the 2024-2025 school year, it might be something like 09/05/2024. signal from a useless one: * **Narrow and grounded.** * one checkable yes/no about one field against the source (e.g. "is this value absent from the source?"), not a vague "is this extraction good?" * vague questions give mushy, uncalibrated scores * **Bad = TRUE, with explicit criteria.** * frame each question so the *escalate* case is the `true` case, and state what `true`/`false` mean * **Per-field, then aggregate with `max`.** * a per-field flag localizes the error and stays sparse and strong * `max` ("any flag fires") ensures one confident red flag escalates, instead of being averaged into silence * **Independent and cheap.** * a dedicated verifier (here, TypeSafe) judging the output catches the extractor's own blind spots * it has to be cheap, or there are no savings left function names and closed-set arguments to confidence-aware TypeSafe questions. When you order a "large iced oat latte, no sweetener," the barista does not write your sentence down. They mark four options on a cup. This cookbook does the same thing for a trading API: a sentence goes in, and out comes a function name and its arguments as evaluated enums, each with a confidence. ```text theme={null} "plot rolling correlation between nvda and spy for the past month" rolling_correlation(symbol='NVDA', benchmark='SPY', window='1mo') confidence 0.91 "compare nvda amd and msft over the past three months" compare_returns(symbols=['NVDA', 'AMD', 'MSFT'], window='3mo') confidence 0.94 "show me apple daily with volume" plot_price(symbol='AAPL', resolution='1d', include_volume=True) confidence 0.75 "what tickers do you have" list_symbols() confidence 1.00 ``` Those calls go to ten ordinary functions in a trading assistant. Their arguments take values from fixed lists, so they are `Literal`s already: [code omitted] An argument whose values come from a fixed list is a closed set. When it takes one value out of that list, it gets a `Choice` question over exactly those values, so whatever reaches the function is a value the function accepts. You leave the functions alone. What you add is a spec that says in plain words what each argument means. By the end you have a `Dispatcher` you can point at your own functions. ## Setup ```bash theme={null} pip install ipython polars matplotlib numpy "typesafe-sdk>=0.5.7" cooksafe --extra-index-url https://pypi.typesafe.ai/ ``` Set `TYPESAFE_API_KEY`. Two modules sit beside this file. `trader.py` holds the ten functions, plus a TypeSafe client that reads answers from a cache, so re-rendering replays the numbers below without calling the API. `dispatch.py` holds the code that reads a signature and a spec and makes the call. [code omitted] ``` 10 functions over 156,780 one-minute bars ``` ## Find the closed sets in the signatures The type hints already say which arguments come from a fixed list, and what is in each list. `closed_sets` reads a signature and sorts those arguments into three shapes: a **choice** (a `Literal`, so one value out of the list), a **set** (a `list[Literal[...]]`, so any number of them), or a **flag** (a `bool`, so on or off). All ten functions are defined in `trader.py`. [code omitted] ``` list_symbols 0 market_summary 1 window:choice plot_price 7 symbol:choice, style:choice, resolution:choice, window:choice, include_volume:flag, moving_average:choice, log_scale:flag intraday_pattern 3 symbol:choice, window:choice, metric:choice compare_returns 3 symbols:set, window:choice, normalize:flag rolling_correlation 4 symbol:choice, benchmark:choice, window:choice, resolution:choice summary_stats 2 symbol:choice, window:choice volatility 3 symbol:choice, window:choice, annualized:flag top_movers 2 window:choice, direction:choice drawdown 3 symbol:choice, window:choice, plot:flag 28 fillable arguments in total ``` `top_movers` shows what gets left out. Of its three arguments, two are closed sets. The third, `limit`, is an `int`, so it never gets a question and keeps its default of 3. Free text, numbers and dates work the same way: no question, and the function's default stands. ## Write the spec The `Literal` gives you the strings `"1mo"` and `"3mo"`. It does not say that a user typing "this quarter" means the second one. The spec says that. It holds a question per argument, a line per option, a description per function, and one more question that picks between the functions. It lives in `spec.json`, and an LLM can write it for you from the signatures. [code omitted] ``` { "style": { "question": "Does the user want a plain line or candles?", "stated": "Does the user say how the chart should be drawn, such as a line, candles, or OHLC bars?", "options": { "line": "a simple line through the closing prices", "candles": "a candlestick or OHLC chart, showing each bar's open, high, low and close" } } } { "moving_average": { "question": "How many bars should the moving average cover - nine, twenty, or fifty?", "stated": "Does the user ask for a moving average or a smoothed line over the candles?", "options": { "9": "a nine-bar moving average, a fast one", "20": "a twenty-bar moving average", "50": "a fifty-bar moving average, a slow one" } } } ``` The option keys are the strings the function takes, so nothing has to map a label back to an argument afterwards. `stated` makes an argument optional. It is a second yes/no question asking whether the command says anything about that argument at all. When the answer is no, the call leaves that argument out and the function's own default applies. A set argument gets its question once per member, with `{}` standing in for the member name. `"Does the user want {} in the comparison?"` becomes one question per ticker. Write each question about the idea rather than the words a user might pick, because the match is on meaning: "is amd tracking nvidia lately" reaches `rolling_correlation` even though neither *tracking* nor *lately* appears anywhere in `spec.json`. Avoid naming a question after its parameter - `"Which resolution?"` gives the command nothing to match against. ## Turn the spec into questions `Dispatcher` builds the questions from the spec once. Each command is then one request carrying the choice of function and every function's arguments, and the dispatcher reads only the chosen function's answers. [code omitted] ``` 54 questions per command, among them: __tool__ choice What is the user asking the trading assistant to do? plot_price.style choice Does the user want a plain line or candles? plot_price.style? noul Does the user say how the chart should be drawn, such as a line, compare_returns.symbols.NVDA noul Does the user want NVDA in the comparison? ``` ## Run fourteen commands A request occupies one line, and its `confidence` is the least certain judgement behind that call. This cookbook takes plain text whose markup has been stripped (lines hard-wrapped mid-sentence, no heading markers, no list bullets) and reconstructs the structure as Markdown: headings, paragraphs, lists, quotes, code, callouts. The input is a team memo in exactly that state. A text-generation model could rewrite the text into Markdown, but a rewrite can also change the words. Here the model never generates text: it answers narrow questions about the document (*does this line pick up mid-sentence? what kind of content is this block?*), and code does the rendering, so every character of the output comes from the input, and every judgment carries a probability. The whole pipeline is two API requests per document, run in sequence: * **Pass 1, stitch:** one `Noul` question (a yes/no question whose answer is the probability that yes is correct) per adjacent pair of lines, asking whether the line break split a sentence across the two. All the pairs go in a single request, and lines that continue a split sentence get merged back into blocks. * **Pass 2, classify:** one `Choice` question (pick one option from a list, with a probability for every option) per merged block, choosing among heading, paragraph, list item, quote, code, or callout (a note, tip, or warning set apart from the main text). The blocks only exist once pass 1 has answered, so this is a second request; it also carries companion questions for every block (heading level, step order, callout kind) whose answers are read only when the block's type makes them relevant. * **Direct evidence stays in code.** Blank lines and explicit markers (`- `, `1.`, `#`) are read in code, never sent to the model to reconsider; this memo kept its blank lines but lost every marker. The model gets only the questions code cannot answer from the text. All of the behavior is specified in the pass-2 question criteria: three dicts of one-line descriptions, plus the step question's true/false criteria inside `classify_questions`. The rest of the code is plumbing around them. The cost and latency numbers are in the appendix: two round trips, 10,211 tokens, 0.8s, \$0.0015 for this memo. ## Setup ```bash theme={null} pip install ipython "typesafe-sdk>=0.5.7" cooksafe --extra-index-url https://pypi.typesafe.ai/ ``` then set `TYPESAFE_API_KEY`. Every API call is cached in `json_cache.json`, which ships with the cookbook, so re-rendering replays the published numbers without calling the API. Delete that file to re-run everything live. The question is deliberately narrow ("does this line pick up mid-sentence?"), which is close to an objective fact about the text. The appendix covers both the wording choice and how the merge thresholds were derived. ```python expandable theme={null} def join_question(i: int) -> Noul: return Noul( instructions=f"Does line {line_id(i)} pick up mid-sentence, continuing a sentence left unfinished at the end of line {line_id(i - 1)}?", criteria=NoulCriteria( true="The line starts in the middle of a sentence that began on the previous line - the line break tore the sentence apart", false="The line begins a new sentence, item, heading, or thought of its own", ), ) @json_cache def stitch(wording: str = "mid-sentence") -> dict: make = join_question if wording == "mid-sentence" else naive_join_question questions = {line_id(i): make(i) for i in range(1, len(LINES)) if not LINES[i]["gap"]} started = perf_counter() response = client.system_one( state=tag(LINES, "L"), questions=questions, model=TYPESAFE_MODEL ) return { "joins": [ response.answers[line_id(i)].noul if line_id(i) in response.answers else 0.0 for i in range(len(LINES)) ], "seconds": round(perf_counter() - started, 2), "usage": [response.usage.input_tokens, response.usage.output_tokens], } result = stitch() print(f"{sum(1 for l in LINES if not l['gap']) - 1} pair questions, one request, " f"{result['seconds']}s") ``` ``` 16 pair questions, one request, 0.32s ``` The cutoff for merging depends on how the previous line ends. After a dangling line (one with no sentence-ending punctuation), a join probability of 0.2 or above merges the pair; after terminal punctuation (`.` `!` `?` `:` `;`), the cutoff rises to 0.5. The appendix walks through the probabilities behind the two numbers. 1339	# Date extraction
1340	
1341	> Extracts absolute and relative dates by asking TypeSafe for the parts named in a document, then resolving and validating them in code with confidence-based review.
1342	
1343	*Read a date's parts off the text with TypeSafe, then resolve them to a `date` in code.*
1344	
1345	The function you build here, `extract_date(document, role)`, takes a document and a
1346	phrase naming the date you want, such as "the deadline to return the form", and hands
1347	back a `date` with a confidence. It flags a low-confidence read, and one whose parts do
1348	not add up to a date at all, including a date the document never states. The date can be
1349	spelled out ("August 14, 2027") or written relative to today ("tomorrow", "next
1350	Thursday").
1351	
1352	TypeSafe answers `Choice` questions about the date in one call: what kind of date it is,
1353	and
1354	which month, day, year, or weekday the text names. Code turns those answers into a `date`.
1355	The model reads what the text says and never does the calendar math.
1356	
1357	The cells below run that function over four short documents, print each date with its
1358	confidence, and split the results into the ones code accepts and the ones a person should
1359	look at.
1360	
1361	*TypeSafe reads how the date is written and which parts the text names. Code turns those
1362	answers into a `date`, counting from today when the date is relative, and either accepts
1363	it or sends it to review.*
1364	
1365	## Setup
1366	
1367	```bash theme={null}
1368	pip install ipython "typesafe-sdk>=0.5.7" cooksafe --extra-index-url https://pypi.typesafe.ai/
1369	```
1370	
1371	then set `TYPESAFE_API_KEY`.
1372

1377	## The questions
1378	
1379	Seven `Choice` questions go out in one call. `mode` says how the date is written:
1380	`absolute`
1381	for a date that names a month, `relative` for one written relative to today, and `none`
1382	when the document does not state the date at all.
1383	
1384	The other six read the pieces. An absolute date needs `month`, `day`, and `year`. A
1385	relative one needs `day_anchor`: today, tomorrow, the day after, or a named weekday. When
1386	it names a weekday, `weekday` and `week_offset` say which one and which week. Code reads
1387	only the pieces `mode` calls for.
1388	
1389	`year` lists one option per year from 1900 to 2050, plus two escapes. `none` means the text
1390	states no year and code fills one in. `out_of_range` means the text states a year outside
1391	the list, and code flags that instead of guessing. If a list that long bothers you, pull
1392	the year-like numbers out of the text first and offer the model only those.

1534	# Pre-parsed value extraction
1535	
1536	> Uses regexes to find candidate emails, phone numbers, and amounts, then has TypeSafe select the requested span so code can normalize a verbatim value.
1537	
1538	*A regex finds the candidate values, TypeSafe picks the one the question asks for,
1539	and code copies it verbatim.*
1540	
1541	The `find` and `pick` pair here is one you can point at your own documents, and three
1542	worked cases show it in use: the address a sender wants their receipt sent to, a phone
1543	number as `+14155550177`, and an invoice total as `1315.50 USD` flagged as a charge.
1544	
1545	TypeSafe picks one of the options you hand it, so the candidates have to be found
1546	first. A regex finds them, TypeSafe picks one, and code copies the pick, in three steps:
1547	
1548	1. A regex finds the candidate values in the text. Tune it to over-find.
1549	2. TypeSafe picks which candidate the question is asking for, and reads off any
1550	   attribute the code needs downstream (currency, country, whether an amount is a
1551	   credit or a charge).
1552	3. The code copies the picked value and normalizes it.
1553	
1554	Because TypeSafe only ever chooses among the spans the regex found, the value you get
1555	back is one of those spans, copied unchanged. It cannot invent a value or transpose a
1556	digit.
1557	
1558	*The regex finds candidate values in the document, TypeSafe picks one, and downstream
1559	code normalizes it and acts on it.*

1571	## Helpers
1572	
1573	`find` runs a regex tuned to over-find and dedupes the matches. `pick` is a
1574	`Choice` question whose options are the spans `find` returns, so its answer is one of
1575	those spans copied exactly, or `none` when no candidate fits. `classify` is a
1576	`Choice` question over a fixed set of labels, used here for the currency and the
1577	country.
1578	`is_true` is a `Noul`, used here to ask whether an amount is a credit.
1579	
1580	Every call is cached to `json_cache.json`, so re-rendering makes no API calls.
1581	
1582	```python expandable theme={null}
1583	EMAIL_RE = re.compile(r"[A-Za-z0-9._%+-]+@[A-Za-z0-9.-]+\.[A-Za-z]{2,}")
1584	PHONE_RE = re.compile(r"\(?\+?\d[\d\s()\-.]{6,}\d")
1585	MONEY_RE = re.compile(r"[$€£¥]\s?\d[\d,]*(?:\.\d{2})?")
1586	
1587	def find(pattern: re.Pattern, text: str) -> list[str]:
1588	    """Code-side candidate finder: recall-tuned regex, deduped, in document order."""
1589	    seen: set[str] = set()
1590	    out: list[str] = []
1591	    for match in pattern.findall(text):
1592	        span = match.strip()
1593	        if span and span not in seen:
1594	            seen.add(span)
1595	            out.append(span)
1596	    return out
1597	
1598	@json_cache
1599	def pick(document: str, candidates: list[str], question: str) -> dict:
1600	    """TypeSafe selects which found span plays the role. Returns {choice, confidence}.
1601	
1602	    The options ARE the candidate spans, so ``choice`` is a verbatim copy of one of them (or the
1603	    ``none`` hatch) - the model chooses, code owns the string."""
1604	    criteria = {c: None for c in candidates} | {
1605	        NONE: "None of these is the requested value."
1606	    }
1607	    answer = ts.system_one(
1608	        state=document,
1609	        questions={"pick": Choice(instructions=question, criteria=criteria)},
1610	        model=TYPESAFE_MODEL,
1611	    ).answers["pick"]
1612	    return {"choice": answer.choice, "confidence": answer.confidence}
1613	
1614	@json_cache
1615	def classify(document: str, question: str, options: list[str]) -> dict:
1616	    """A small Choice over a fixed label set (currency, country, ...). Returns {choice, confidence}."""
1617	    answer = ts.system_one(
1618	        state=document,
1619	        questions={
1620	            "q": Choice(instructions=question, criteria={o: None for o in options})
1621	        },
1622	        model=TYPESAFE_MODEL,
1623	    ).answers["q"]
1624	    return {"choice": answer.choice, "confidence": answer.confidence}
1625	
1626	@json_cache
1627	def is_true(document: str, question: str) -> float:
1628	    """A yes/no Noul. Returns P(yes)."""
1629	    return (
1630	        ts.system_one(
1631	            state=document,
1632	            questions={"q": Noul(instructions=question)},
1633	            model=TYPESAFE_MODEL,
1634	        )
1635	        .answers["q"]
1636	        .noul
1637	    )
1638	```

1659	
1660	Three numbers, none of them carrying a country code. TypeSafe picks the mobile and
1661	reads the country from the text; `phonenumbers` combines those two answers into E.164,
1662	the international format that starts with a `+` and the country code.

1664	[code omitted]

1677	## Money: pick the amount, classify the currency, flag credit vs charge
1678	
1679	An invoice with four amounts on it. TypeSafe picks the total due and the credit, reads
1680	the currency, and flags each picked amount as a charge or a credit. The code copies each
1681	picked string and parses it into a `Decimal`.
1682	
1683	[code omitted]

1685	```
1686	total due : $1,315.50  -> 1315.50 USD (charge, P(credit)=0.01)
1687	credit    : $50.00     -> 50.00 USD (credit, P(credit)=0.99)
1688	
1689	candidates : ['$1,200.00', '$115.50', '$1,315.50', '$50.00']

1693	`Noul` answers 0.01 on the total and 0.99 on the credit, so the code knows the
1694	sign of each `Decimal` it parses.

1697	> holds for `$1,315.50`; in `€1.315,50` it is the other way round. Ask a `Noul` question
1698	> which convention the document uses, and branch on it in code.

1726	## Two limits
1727	
1728	* A `Choice` question allows at most 255 options. With more candidates than that, narrow
1729	  in two
1730	  stages: pick the section first, then the span inside it.
1731	* Finding the candidates is the part that takes work. Emails, phone numbers and amounts
1732	  have regexes that cover them; a name does not, so its candidates have to come from a
1733	  roster you already have, or from a named-entity recognizer or an LLM that proposes
1734	  them. TypeSafe then picks the one the question asks for.

1740	# Self-consistency: nouls
1741	
1742	> Route uncertain probabilities to human review while keeping the underlying noul values visible.
1743	
1744	This cookbook takes one auto-insurance claim, runs a 14-question rubric over it 15 times,
1745	and checks whether each answer holds still across the repeats. Every check is a
1746	`Noul`, so each answer is P(true) for one True/False question. In a claims-triage
1747	pipeline, which sorts incoming claims into pay, deny, or send-to-a-human, probabilities
1748	guide the decision. Small changes near a threshold can change which action is taken.
1749	
1750	The rubric is 14 `Noul` questions, and each run is one call that answers all 14. We do
1751	`NUM_SAMPLES` = 15 repeats per condition, where a condition is one model plus one setting,
1752	and show every probability that came back.
1753	
1754	The conditions:
1755	
1756	* Non-reasoning LLMs `claude-haiku-4-5` and `gpt-5.4-mini`, at temperature `0` and the
1757	  API default.
1758	* The same two non-reasoning models in True/False mode: one bare yes or no per question,
1759	  mapped to 1.0 and 0.0.
1760	* Reasoning LLMs `gpt-5.5` and `claude-opus-4-8`, which have no temperature dial.
1761	* TypeSafe: one `system_one` call over the 14 `Noul` questions, with a fresh `uid` field
1762	  (a throwaway unique value) on each call.
1763	
1764	What to look for: the LLM answers move from run to run, at temperature `0` too, and on the
1765	judgment calls the models disagree with *themselves*. TypeSafe's mean per-question
1766	probability standard deviation is `0.0102`, below all LLM probability conditions here.
1767	Its `covered` answers span `0.43` to `0.53`, crossing a `0.5` decision threshold.
1768	
1769	We also turn probabilities from `0.30` through `0.70` into an explicit `uncertain` outcome
1770	for human review. The final illustration maps TypeSafe probabilities to these actions
1771	while keeping the underlying probabilities visible.
1772

1803	## The rubric: 14 `Noul` questions
1804	
1805	One `key -> question` entry per row, phrased so a yes means the thing we are checking for
1806	is true. That keeps every row comparable: each model's probability and TypeSafe's `noul`
1807	measure the same thing.
1808	
1809	```python theme={null}
1810	QUESTIONS = {
1811	    "covered": "Is the loss covered under the policy's collision coverage?",
1812	    "exclusion": "Does a policy exclusion apply to this loss?",
1813	    "on_circuit": "Did the collision happen while the vehicle was being driven on the racetrack itself?",
1814	    "deductible": "Would the $500 deductible be correctly applied before any payout?",
1815	    "docs_sufficient": "Is the attached documentation sufficient to adjudicate the claim as-is?",
1816	    "within_limit": "Is the amount claimed within the per-incident coverage limit?",
1817	    "within_window": "Did the loss occur within the policy's active coverage period?",
1818	    "reported_timely": "Was the loss reported within the policy's required window?",
1819	    "rental_eligible": "Is the rental-car cost eligible for reimbursement under this policy?",
1820	    "fraud_flag": "Are there indicators that warrant a fraud review?",
1821	    "human_review": "Was payment approved by automated triage without a human adjuster's review?",
1822	    "manual_review": "Should this claim be routed for manual/supervisor review before payout?",
1823	    "line_items_sum": "Do the claimed line-item costs add up to the total amount claimed?",
1824	    "subrogation": "Is there a potentially at-fault third party the insurer could pursue for subrogation recovery?",
1825	}

1828	## How we ask
1829	
1830	Each LLM call is one prompt holding `json.dumps(CLAIM)` and all 14 questions. The model
1831	returns a JSON object mapping each question's key to a probability. Calls route to
1832	Anthropic or OpenAI by model name: non-reasoning models take a `temperature` (`0` or the
1833	API default), reasoning models think first and take no temperature.
1834	
1835	The non-reasoning models also run a True/False variant: they answer each question with a
1836	bare yes or no, which we map to 1.0 and 0.0. This forces a hard decision and shows what
1837	these models do when they cannot leave any mass in the uncertain middle.
1838	
1839	The TypeSafe call is one `system_one` request over the same claim and the same 14 `Noul`
1840	questions. Each answer's `noul` is P(true).
1841	
1842	Every query also gets a fresh `uid`, a throwaway unique value that changes each run while
1843	leaving the claim and rubric unchanged. It appears in the LLM prompt and as an extra field
1844	in the TypeSafe state. This setup cannot separate sensitivity to the irrelevant field
1845	from variation that would occur on identical requests.
1846	
1847	> **Note:** despite the "ONLY a JSON object" instruction, `claude-haiku-4-5` wraps nearly >
1848	> every reply in a ` ```json ... ``` ` fence that strict `json.loads` rejects > (the
1849	> other models return bare JSON). The helper peels the fence; a reply that still fails > to
1850	> parse becomes a parse failure, counted but not scored.
1851	
1852	Each helper returns the answer, an estimated cost, and the round-trip latency.
1853	
1854	````python expandable theme={null}
1855	def rubric_prompt(mode: str, sample_index: int) -> str:
1856	    """The claim + all 14 questions in one prompt; ``mode`` picks the answer format.
1857	
1858	    ``mode="prob"`` asks for a probability per question, ``mode="yesno"`` for a bare True/False.
1859	    ``sample_index`` seeds the uid buster so every repeat is a distinct, independent draw."""
1860	    if mode == "yesno":
1861	        answer_format = (
1862	            "\n\nAnswer each question yes or no.\n"
1863	            "Respond with ONLY a JSON object mapping each question's key to "
1864	            '"yes" or "no", with one entry per question.'
1865	        )
1866	    else:
1867	        answer_format = (
1868	            "\n\nFor each question, give your probability that the answer is yes.\n"
1869	            "Respond with ONLY a JSON object mapping each question's key to a number "
1870	            "between 0.00 and 1.00, with one entry per question."
1871	        )
1872	    return (
1873	        f"uid: {sample_index}:{token_hex(4)}\n\n"
1874	        f"Document (an auto-insurance claim):\n{json.dumps(CLAIM, indent=2)}\n\nQuestions:\n"
1875	        + "\n".join(f"- {key}: {question}" for key, question in QUESTIONS.items())
1876	        + answer_format
1877	    )
1878	
1879	def _cost(prices: tuple[float, float], input_tokens: int, output_tokens: int) -> float:
1880	    return input_tokens / 1e6 * prices[0] + output_tokens / 1e6 * prices[1]
1881	
1882	def _call_llm(model: str, prompt: str, temperature: float | None):
1883	    """One LLM call -> (text, cost_usd, latency_s), routed by model name."""
1884	    reasoning = model in REASONING_MODELS
1885	    started = perf_counter()
1886	    if model.startswith("claude"):
1887	        kwargs = {
1888	            "model": model,
1889	            "max_tokens": 4096,
1890	            "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": prompt}],
1891	        }
1892	        if reasoning:
1893	            kwargs["thinking"] = {"type": "adaptive"}
1894	        elif temperature is not None:
1895	            kwargs["temperature"] = temperature
1896	        response = anthropic_client.messages.create(**kwargs)
1897	        text = next((b.text for b in response.content if b.type == "text"), "")
1898	        usage = (response.usage.input_tokens, response.usage.output_tokens)
1899	    else:
1900	        kwargs = {"model": model, "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": prompt}]}
1901	        if reasoning:
1902	            kwargs["reasoning_effort"] = "high"
1903	        elif temperature is not None:
1904	            kwargs["temperature"] = temperature
1905	        response = openai_client.chat.completions.create(**kwargs)
1906	        text = response.choices[0].message.content
1907	        usage = (response.usage.prompt_tokens, response.usage.completion_tokens)
1908	    return text, _cost(LLM_PRICES[model], *usage), perf_counter() - started
1909	
1910	# All samples (LLM and TypeSafe) are cached to ``json_cache.json``, which ships with the cookbook, so
1911	# re-rendering reproduces the published numbers with no API spend. ``sample_index`` is part of the
1912	# cache key, so each of the NUM_SAMPLES repeats is its own independent draw. Delete the file to
1913	# re-sample live.
1914	json_cache = JsonCache(Path("json_cache.json"))
1915	
1916	def _rubric_fingerprint() -> str:
1917	    """Short digest of everything that shapes the prompt/rubric: the state and every question's
1918	    text. Passed into the cached calls below so that editing the claim or any question changes the
1919	    cache key and forces a fresh sample, instead of silently serving a stale answer that was
1920	    generated for the old wording."""
1921	    payload = json.dumps([CLAIM, QUESTIONS], sort_keys=True, default=str)
1922	    return hashlib.sha256(payload.encode()).hexdigest()[:12]
1923	
1924	RUBRIC_HASH = _rubric_fingerprint()
1925	
1926	@json_cache
1927	def _call_typesafe(sample_index: int, rubric_hash: str, model: str):
1928	    """Return nouls, token usage, latency, and model metadata for one call.
1929	
1930	    ``rubric_hash`` and ``model`` prevent reuse across rubric or model changes.
1931	    Preserve the returned model because an alias can resolve to a different version later.
1932	    """
1933	    questions = {
1934	        key: Noul(instructions=question) for key, question in QUESTIONS.items()
1935	    }
1936	    started = perf_counter()
1937	    response = typesafe_client.system_one(
1938	        model=model,
1939	        state={"uid": f"{sample_index}:{token_hex(4)}", "claim": CLAIM},
1940	        questions=questions,
1941	    )
1942	    nouls = {key: response.answers[key].noul for key in QUESTIONS}
1943	    return (
1944	        nouls,
1945	        response.usage.input_tokens,
1946	        response.usage.output_tokens,
1947	        perf_counter() - started,
1948	        {"requested_model": model, "response_model": response.model},
1949	    )
1950	
1951	def _parse_answer(answer: object, mode: str) -> float:
1952	    """One raw per-question answer -> a probability; NaN if missing or unusable.
1953	
1954	    ``mode="prob"`` reads the answer as a number; ``mode="yesno"`` maps True/False to 1.0 / 0.0.
1955	    Anything else -- a missing key, a non-number, a reply that is neither yes nor no -- is NaN,
1956	    never a legitimate-looking value."""
1957	    if answer is None:
1958	        return float("nan")
1959	    if mode == "yesno":
1960	        text = str(answer).strip().lower()
1961	        if text == "yes":
1962	            return 1.0
1963	        if text == "no":
1964	            return 0.0
1965	        return float("nan")
1966	    try:
1967	        return float(answer)
1968	    except (TypeError, ValueError):
1969	        return float("nan")
1970	
1971	@json_cache
1972	def ask_llm_rubric(
1973	    model: str,
1974	    mode: str,
1975	    temperature: float | None,
1976	    sample_index: int,
1977	    rubric_hash: str,
1978	):
1979	    """One LLM rubric query -> (per-question probabilities keyed by question key, cost_usd,
1980	    latency_s); NaNs where the reply doesn't parse. ``rubric_hash`` is unused in the body -- callers
1981	    pass ``RUBRIC_HASH`` so an edited state/rubric busts the cache instead of serving a stale
1982	    answer."""
1983	    prompt = rubric_prompt(mode, sample_index)
1984	    text, cost, latency = _call_llm(model, prompt, temperature)
1985	    # Peel a single ```json ... ``` fence (claude-haiku-4-5 adds one despite "ONLY a JSON object").
1986	    stripped = text.strip()
1987	    if stripped.startswith("```"):
1988	        stripped = stripped[stripped.find("\n") + 1 :] if "\n" in stripped else ""
1989	        if stripped.rstrip().endswith("```"):
1990	            stripped = stripped.rstrip()[: -len("```")]
1991	    try:
1992	        raw = json.loads(stripped)
1993	    except (ValueError, json.JSONDecodeError):
1994	        raw = {}
1995	    raw = raw if isinstance(raw, dict) else {}
1996	    values = {key: _parse_answer(raw.get(key), mode) for key in QUESTIONS}
1997	    return values, cost, latency
1998	````

2077	## Allow an uncertain decision instead of forcing yes or no
2078	
2079	With a threshold of `0.5`, probabilities `0.49` and `0.51` cause opposite actions even
2080	though both express substantial uncertainty. The application can instead return:
2081

2084	* `yes` above `0.70`.

2086	Uncertain cases go to a human. The escalation is application logic over the returned
2087	probability: no new question, no second API call. The band is illustrative; it is neither
2088	a calibrated guarantee nor an optimized threshold. Set production boundaries from labeled
2089	examples and from the cost of incorrect decisions and of review.

2123	# Self-consistency: choices
2124	
2125	> Add an uncertain outcome to moderation decisions and compare label agreement with the share of automatic actions.
2126	
2127	This cookbook takes one borderline user post, runs a moderation rubric over it 15 times,
2128	and checks whether each answer holds still across the repeats. Every check is a
2129	`Choice`, so each answer is one label from a fixed set. In a moderation pipeline
2130	that label is the routing decision: remove or leave up, escalate or auto-resolve, send to
2131	the threat, spam, or general queue. When the label wobbles from one run to the next, the
2132	same post routes to different places for no good reason.
2133	
2134	The rubric is 8 `Choice` questions, and each run is one call that answers all 8. We do
2135	15
2136	repeats per condition, where a condition is one model plus one setting, and plot every
2137	label that came back.
2138	
2139	The conditions:
2140	
2141	* Non-reasoning LLMs `claude-haiku-4-5` and `gpt-5.4-mini`, at temperature `0` and the
2142	  API default.
2143	* Reasoning LLMs `gpt-5.5` and `claude-opus-4-8`, which have no temperature dial.
2144	* TypeSafe: one `system_one` call over the 8 `Choice` questions, with a fresh `uid`
2145	  field (a
2146	  throwaway unique value) on each call, matching the noul cookbook setup.
2147	
2148	What to look for: picked labels can flip inside a single condition, including TypeSafe,
2149	and conditions disagree with each other.
2150	
2151	In this run the LLM distribution settings repeat their plurality labels 87.5% to 100% of
2152	the time, compared with TypeSafe's 90.8%. TypeSafe has lower mean probability variation
2153	than five of the six LLM distribution conditions; Haiku at temperature 0 varies less.
2154	Close probabilities still permit routing changes: TypeSafe flips on 2 of the 8 questions.
2155	
2156	For application decisions, we also require a top probability of at least `0.60`; otherwise
2157	the result is `uncertain` and goes to human review. TypeSafe's agreement then rises to
2158	99.2%, with automatic labels on 74.2% of answers. We show the raw outputs and apply the
2159	same threshold to LLM probability conditions, keeping abstentions and changes visible.
2160

2257	## How we ask
2258	
2259	Each LLM call is one prompt holding `json.dumps(POST)`, all 8 questions, and every allowed
2260	label. There are two answer formats. In distribution mode the model returns one JSON object
2261	per question with a probability on each label. In single-pick mode it returns one bare
2262	label per question, and our analysis puts all the probability mass on that label.
2263	
2264	The TypeSafe call is one `system_one` request over the same post and the same 8
2265	`Choice` questions, returning one distribution per question.
2266	
2267	Every query also gets a fresh `uid`, a throwaway unique value that changes each run while
2268	leaving the post and rubric unchanged. It appears in the LLM prompt and as an extra field
2269	in the TypeSafe state. This setup cannot separate sensitivity to the irrelevant field
2270	from variation that would occur on identical requests.
2271	
2272	Each helper returns the answer, an estimated cost, and the round-trip latency.
2273	
2274	````python expandable theme={null}
2275	def argmax_label(values: list, labels: list[str]) -> str | None:
2276	    """The label with the most probability mass, or ``None`` if any value is missing or
2277	    non-numeric -- a partially parsed distribution never yields a confident-looking pick."""
2278	    numeric = [_numeric_value(value) for value in values]
2279	    if any(value is None for value in numeric):
2280	        return None
2281	    return labels[int(np.argmax(numeric))]
2282	
2283	def choice_decision_with_uncertainty(values: list, labels: list[str]) -> str | None:
2284	    """Abstain below the action threshold; retain invalid results as parse failures."""
2285	    label = argmax_label(values, labels)
2286	    if label is None:
2287	        return None
2288	    probabilities = [float(value) for value in values]
2289	    if any(value < 0 or value > 1 for value in probabilities):
2290	        return None
2291	    return label if max(probabilities) >= MIN_CHOICE_PROBABILITY else "uncertain"
2292	
2293	def choice_decision_annotation(values: list, labels: list[str]) -> str:
2294	    """Show the application decision and top probability in a heatmap cell."""
2295	    decision = choice_decision_with_uncertainty(values, labels)
2296	    if decision is None:
2297	        return ""
2298	    probability = max(float(value) for value in values)
2299	    probability_text = f"{probability:.2f}".removeprefix("0")
2300	    return f"{decision} {probability_text}"
2301	
2302	def _numeric_value(value: object) -> float | None:
2303	    """A finite numeric value, or ``None`` if the model emitted something unusable."""
2304	    try:
2305	        numeric = float(value)
2306	    except (TypeError, ValueError):
2307	        return None
2308	    return numeric if np.isfinite(numeric) else None
2309	
2310	def parse_distribution(raw: object, labels: list[str]) -> list[float]:
2311	    """Map a model's already-parsed per-question reply to per-label probabilities, in label order
2312	    (distribution-mode answers left un-normalized).
2313	
2314	    A single-pick reply is a single label string -> all the mass on that exact label; a
2315	    distribution-mode reply is a dict read label by label. Anything that doesn't match a known label
2316	    or isn't a finite number is left NaN -- we report the gap rather than massaging the reply (e.g.
2317	    stripping an echoed description) to make it fit."""
2318	    if isinstance(raw, str):  # single-pick mode: a single chosen label
2319	        if raw in labels:
2320	            return [1.0 if label == raw else 0.0 for label in labels]
2321	        return [float("nan")] * len(labels)
2322	    if not isinstance(raw, dict):
2323	        return [float("nan")] * len(labels)
2324	    return [
2325	        value if (value := _numeric_value(raw.get(label))) is not None else float("nan")
2326	        for label in labels
2327	    ]
2328	
2329	def rubric_prompt(mode: str, sample_index: int, rubric_hash: str) -> str:
2330	    """The post + all questions (with their label sets) in one prompt; ``mode`` picks the format.
2331	
2332	    ``mode="dist"`` asks for a probability distribution over each question's labels; the single-pick
2333	    mode (``mode="single"``) asks for a single label per question. The uid line combines
2334	    ``rubric_hash`` (which rubric version) with ``sample_index`` and a random token, so every repeat
2335	    is a distinct, independent draw and two different rubrics never share a nonce."""
2336	    lines = []
2337	    for key, (instructions, choices) in QUESTIONS.items():
2338	        labels = "\n".join(f"     {label}: {desc}" for label, desc in choices.items())
2339	        lines.append(f"- {key}: {instructions}\n   labels:\n{labels}")
2340	    exclusivity = (
2341	        "\n\nEach question's labels are mutually exclusive: exactly one applies. If a post could "
2342	        "arguably fit more than one, pick the single most severe / most specific label per the "
2343	        "label descriptions."
2344	    )
2345	    if mode == "single":
2346	        answer_format = (
2347	            "\n\nFor each question, pick exactly ONE label.\nRespond with ONLY a JSON object "
2348	            "mapping each question's key to one of that question's bare labels (the label only, "
2349	            "not its description), with one entry per question."
2350	        )
2351	    else:
2352	        answer_format = (
2353	            "\n\nFor each question, give a probability distribution over that question's labels "
2354	            "(values 0.00-1.00 that sum to 1).\nRespond with ONLY a JSON object mapping each "
2355	            "question's key to an object mapping that question's bare labels (the label only, "
2356	            "not its description) to probabilities, with one entry per question."
2357	        )
2358	    return (
2359	        f"uid: {rubric_hash}:{sample_index}:{token_hex(4)}\n\n"
2360	        f"Document (a reported user post):\n{json.dumps(POST, indent=2)}\n\nQuestions:\n"
2361	        + "\n".join(lines)
2362	        + exclusivity
2363	        + answer_format

2366	def _cost(prices: tuple[float, float], input_tokens: int, output_tokens: int) -> float:
2367	    return input_tokens / 1e6 * prices[0] + output_tokens / 1e6 * prices[1]

2369	def _call_llm(model: str, prompt: str, temperature: float | None):
2370	    """One LLM call -> (text, cost_usd, latency_s), routed by model name."""
2371	    reasoning = model in REASONING_MODELS
2372	    started = perf_counter()
2373	    if model.startswith("claude"):
2374	        kwargs = {
2375	            "model": model,
2376	            "max_tokens": 4096,
2377	            "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": prompt}],
2378	        }
2379	        if reasoning:
2380	            kwargs["thinking"] = {"type": "adaptive"}
2381	        elif temperature is not None:
2382	            kwargs["temperature"] = temperature
2383	        response = anthropic_client.messages.create(**kwargs)
2384	        text = next((b.text for b in response.content if b.type == "text"), "")
2385	        usage = (response.usage.input_tokens, response.usage.output_tokens)
2386	    else:
2387	        kwargs = {"model": model, "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": prompt}]}
2388	        if reasoning:

2394	        usage = (response.usage.prompt_tokens, response.usage.completion_tokens)

2398	# re-rendering is instant and reproduces the published numbers with no API spend. ``sample_index``

2404	def _rubric_fingerprint() -> str:
2405	    """Short digest of everything that shapes the prompt/rubric: the state and every question's
2406	    text and label set. Passed into the cached calls below so that editing the post or any question
2407	    changes the cache key and forces a fresh sample, instead of silently serving a stale answer that
2408	    was generated for the old wording."""
2409	    payload = json.dumps([POST, QUESTIONS], sort_keys=True, default=str)
2410	    return hashlib.sha256(payload.encode()).hexdigest()[:12]
2411	
2412	RUBRIC_HASH = _rubric_fingerprint()

2414	@json_cache
2415	def _call_typesafe(sample_index: int, rubric_hash: str, model: str):
2416	    """Return distributions, token usage, latency, and model metadata for one call.
2417	
2418	    ``rubric_hash`` and ``model`` prevent reuse across rubric or model changes.
2419	    Preserve the returned model because an alias can resolve to a different version later.
2420	    """
2421	    questions = {
2422	        key: Choice(instructions=instructions, criteria=choices)
2423	        for key, (instructions, choices) in QUESTIONS.items()
2424	    }
2425	    started = perf_counter()
2426	    response = typesafe_client.system_one(
2427	        model=model,
2428	        state={"uid": f"{rubric_hash}:{sample_index}:{token_hex(4)}", "post": POST},
2429	        questions=questions,
2430	    )
2431	    distributions = {}
2432	    for key, (_instructions, choices) in QUESTIONS.items():
2433	        probabilities = dict(response.answers[key].probabilities)
2434	        distributions[key] = [
2435	            probabilities.get(label, float("nan")) for label in choices
2436	        ]
2437	    return (
2438	        distributions,
2439	        response.usage.input_tokens,
2440	        response.usage.output_tokens,
2441	        perf_counter() - started,
2442	        {"requested_model": model, "response_model": response.model},
2443	    )
2444	
2445	@json_cache
2446	def ask_llm_rubric(
2447	    model: str,
2448	    mode: str,
2449	    temperature: float | None,
2450	    sample_index: int,
2451	    rubric_hash: str,
2452	):
2453	    """One LLM rubric query -> (per-question label distributions keyed by question key, cost_usd,
2454	    latency_s); NaNs if the reply doesn't parse.
2455	
2456	    ``mode="dist"`` parses 8 label distributions; the single-pick mode (``mode="single"``) parses 8
2457	    single labels and puts all the mass on each. ``rubric_hash`` goes into the prompt's uid nonce
2458	    (and so the cache key), so an edited state/rubric busts the cache instead of serving a stale
2459	    answer."""
2460	    prompt = rubric_prompt(mode, sample_index, rubric_hash)
2461	    text, cost, latency = _call_llm(model, prompt, temperature)
2462	    # Peel a single ```json ... ``` fence (claude-haiku-4-5 sometimes adds one despite "ONLY a JSON
2463	    # object").
2464	    stripped = text.strip()
2465	    if stripped.startswith("```"):
2466	        stripped = stripped[stripped.find("\n") + 1 :] if "\n" in stripped else ""
2467	        if stripped.rstrip().endswith("```"):
2468	            stripped = stripped.rstrip()[: -len("```")]
2469	    try:
2470	        raw = json.loads(stripped)
2471	    except (ValueError, json.JSONDecodeError):
2472	        raw = {}
2473	    if not isinstance(raw, dict):
2474	        raw = {}
2475	    distributions = {
2476	        key: parse_distribution(raw.get(key), list(choices))
2477	        for key, (_instructions, choices) in QUESTIONS.items()
2478	    }
2479	    return distributions, cost, latency

# Date extraction

> Extracts absolute and relative dates by asking TypeSafe for the parts named in a document, then resolving and validating them in code with confidence-based review.

*Read a date's parts off the text with TypeSafe, then resolve them to a `date` in code.*

The function you build here, `extract_date(document, role)`, takes a document and a
phrase naming the date you want, such as "the deadline to return the form", and hands
back a `date` with a confidence. It flags a low-confidence read, and one whose parts do
not add up to a date at all, including a date the document never states. The date can be
spelled out ("August 14, 2027") or written relative to today ("tomorrow", "next
Thursday").

TypeSafe answers `Choice` questions about the date in one call: what kind of date it is,
and
which month, day, year, or weekday the text names. Code turns those answers into a `date`.
The model reads what the text says and never does the calendar math.

The cells below run that function over four short documents, print each date with its
confidence, and split the results into the ones code accepts and the ones a person should
look at.

*TypeSafe reads how the date is written and which parts the text names. Code turns those
answers into a `date`, counting from today when the date is relative, and either accepts
it or sends it to review.*

## Setup

```bash theme={null}
pip install ipython "typesafe-sdk>=0.5.7" cooksafe --extra-index-url https://pypi.typesafe.ai/
```

then set `TYPESAFE_API_KEY`.

[code omitted]

[code omitted]

## The questions

Seven `Choice` questions go out in one call. `mode` says how the date is written:
`absolute`
for a date that names a month, `relative` for one written relative to today, and `none`
when the document does not state the date at all.

The other six read the pieces. An absolute date needs `month`, `day`, and `year`. A
relative one needs `day_anchor`: today, tomorrow, the day after, or a named weekday. When
it names a weekday, `weekday` and `week_offset` say which one and which week. Code reads
only the pieces `mode` calls for.

`year` lists one option per year from 1900 to 2050, plus two escapes. `none` means the text
states no year and code fills one in. `out_of_range` means the text states a year outside
the list, and code flags that instead of guessing. If a list that long bothers you, pull
the year-like numbers out of the text first and offer the model only those.

```python expandable theme={null}
def date_questions(role: str) -> dict[str, Choice]:
    """Seven typed choices that read a date's shape and parts off the text -- no math."""
    absent = "The document does not state this, or it is not this kind of date."
    return {
        "mode": Choice(
            instructions=(
                f"How is {role} written? 'absolute' = a calendar date naming a month (e.g. "
                "'August 14', 'the 3rd of March'); 'relative' = given relative to today (today, "
                "tomorrow, the day after tomorrow, or a named weekday such as 'next Thursday'); "
                "'none' = the document does not state this date."
            ),
            criteria={"absolute": None, "relative": None, "none": None},
        ),
        "month": Choice(
            instructions=f"If {role} is an absolute calendar date, which month is it in?",
            criteria={m: None for m in MONTHS} | {"none": absent},
        ),
        "day": Choice(
            instructions=f"If {role} is an absolute calendar date, which day of the month (1-31)?",
            criteria={str(d): None for d in range(1, 32)} | {"none": absent},
        ),
        "year": Choice(
            instructions=(
                f"If {role} is an absolute calendar date, which year? Pick 'none' if the document "
                "states no year (code infers it), or 'out_of_range' if a year is stated but not "
                "in the list."
            ),
            criteria={str(y): None for y in YEAR_WINDOW}
            | {
                "out_of_range": "A year is stated for this date but is outside the listed range.",
                "none": "No year is stated for this date.",
            },
        ),
        "day_anchor": Choice(
            instructions=(
                f"If {role} is relative to today, which day is it? 'today', 'tomorrow', "
                "'day_after' (the day after tomorrow), or 'weekday' (a named day of the week)."
            ),
            criteria={
                "today": None,
                "tomorrow": None,
                "day_after": None,
                "weekday": None,
                "none": absent,
            },
        ),
        "weekday": Choice(
            instructions=f"If {role} names a day of the week, which one?",
            criteria={w: None for w in WEEKDAYS} | {"none": absent},
        ),
        "week_offset": Choice(
            instructions=(
                f"If {role} names a weekday, which week is it in? 'next' for 'next Thursday' or "
                "'Thursday next week'; 'current' for 'this Thursday'; 'none' for a bare weekday "
                "with no qualifier (just 'Thursday' / 'on Thursday')."
            ),
            criteria={"current": None, "next": None, "none": absent},
        ),
    }
...[truncated]
```

## Resolve it in code

`read_parts` makes the call. `assemble` turns the answers into a `date`: it fills in the
year when the text states none, and it works out which day a named weekday points at. Both
of those count from `TODAY`, which is pinned so relative dates come out the same on every
run. `assemble` also reports the lowest confidence among the parts it used, so a weak
answer on any one part can send the whole date to review.

"next Thursday" can mean two different days, so code decides which. A weekday with no
qualifier means the next one on or after today. `next` means the following calendar week,
and `current` means this week.

[code omitted]

## Run it

Six questions across four short documents: two dates from a contract that states its years,
a form deadline written without a year, a survey that closes "today", a review set for
"next Thursday", and a date the form never mentions. All of them resolve against `TODAY` =
2026-07-30, a Thursday.

[code omitted]

```
   question                              expected    got           conf  flags
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
OK the date the agreement takes effect   2025-01-01  2025-01-01    0.97
OK the date the agreement expires        2027-12-31  2027-12-31    0.91
OK the deadline to return the form       2026-08-14  2026-08-14    0.95
OK the date of the kickoff call          none        none          0.46  <== review  (absolute date incomplete)
OK the date the survey closes            2026-07-30  2026-07-30    0.94
OK the date of the design review         2026-08-06  2026-08-06    0.92
```

The contract states both of its years, so those came off the text. The form states no year,
so code filled in 2026: it takes the current year and moves to the next one only when the
date is already more than a month past. "today" and "next Thursday" went through the same
function as the spelled-out dates.

The kickoff call is the one the form never mentions. There is a date in that form, just not
this one, and the note `absolute date incomplete` means `mode` came back `absolute` with no
month to go with it. The date came back empty, the confidence reads 0.46, and the row is
flagged for a person.

## Confidence to route on

Every answer comes back with a calibrated confidence, and a date's confidence is the lowest
one among the parts that went into it. A date under `REVIEW_BELOW` = 0.60 goes to a person,
and so does a date code could not assemble at all. The rest go straight through.
